The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and bounded in one direction: there are a unit vector $e$ and $a<b$ with $a<x\cdot e<b$ for every $x\in\Omega$. Let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C(p)\,(b-a)\,\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for every $u\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. On $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-hk-and-hk-zero-notation]]) define $$(u,v)_{H^1}:=(u,v)_{L^2}+\sum_{i=1}^n(D_iu,D_iv)_{L^2},$$ with the $L^2$ inner product of [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Then $(\cdot,\cdot)_{H^1}$ is an inner product on the Sobolev classes whose induced norm is the $W^{1,2}$ norm of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], and $H^1(\Omega)$ is a Hilbert space for it. The zero-boundary space $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a closed subspace of $H^1(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]) and hence a Hilbert space for the restricted inner product. The pairing is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, in the convention of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]].

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

For $w\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$, $\int(b\cdot
abla w)w= rac12\int b\cdot
abla(w^2)=0$ by compact support and constant $b$. Approximation in $H_0^1$ extends this identity to every $w\in H_0^1$, because $w\mapsto\int(b\cdot

Scaling [F1] to each triangle $K$ gives $\|v-v_K\|_{L^2(K)}\le C h_K\|
abla v\|_{L^2(K)}$ and $\|v-v_K\|_{L^2(E)}\le C h_K^{1/2}\|
abla v\|_{L^2(K)}$ for every edge $E\subset\partial K$. Shape regularity makes $h_E$ comparable to $h_K$. If $K,L$ share $E$, their traces of $v$ agree, so $|v_K-v_L|\,|E|^{1/2}\le\|v-v_K\|_{L^2(E)}+\|v-v_L\|_{L^2(E)}\le C h_z^{1/2} ig(\|
abla v\|_{L^2(K)}+\|
abla v\|_{L^2(L)} ig).$ Using $|E|^{1/2}\ge c h_z^{1/2}$ for cells in one shape-regular vertex star bounds the difference of neighboring means by the two gradient norms.

The star has at most $N_\Gamma$ cells, and its dual edge graph is connected. Join each cell to a fixed cell by a graph path of length at most $N_\Gamma-1$ and apply step 1.1 along that path. The cell Poincaré bound from step 1.1 then gives $\|v-v_K\|_{L^2(\omega_z)}\le C h_z\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\omega_z)}$. Since $|v_{\omega_z}-v_K|\le|\omega_z|^{-1/2}\|v-v_K\|_{L^2(\omega_z)}$, replacing $v_K$ by the patch mean proves the interior estimate.

For a boundary vertex patch choose one boundary edge $E_0\subset\partial\omega_z$. By the definition of $H_0^1$ as the $H^1$-closure of compactly supported smooth functions, and the continuous local trace bound in [F1], the trace of $v$ is zero on $E_0$. The trace inequality in step 1.1 therefore gives $|v_K|\,|E_0|^{1/2}=\|v-v_K\|_{L^2(E_0)}\le C h_z^{1/2}\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(K)}$ for the incident cell $K$. The same bounded-path comparison of cell means from step 2.1 controls every cell mean in the star by $C\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\omega_z)}$. Summing the cell Poincaré bounds proves the boundary estimate.

For a cell patch $\omega_K$, the three vertex stars are edge-connected because they all contain $K$, and the number of cells is at most three times the valence bound from [F2]. Along each edge-adjacency path, neighboring cell diameters are comparable by shape regularity, so all diameters in the patch are comparable to $h_K$. The mean-zero estimate follows by applying the cell-mean comparison of step 2.1 over this connected finite graph. If $K$ meets the boundary, $\omega_K$ contains a boundary edge; apply the zero-trace argument of step 3.1 there and the same path comparison to all cells in the union. These two estimates are the asserted cell-patch inequalities.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each

A compatible labeled initial mesh is a finite matching affine simplicial triangulation $\mathcal T_0$ of a polygon in $\mathbb R^2$ as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]; matching means distinct cell interiors are disjoint and any shared boundary is a complete common facet. with labels on its edges such that each triangle has one edge labeled $0$ and two labeled $1$, and every shared edge has the same label from both incident triangles. For a descendant triangle of generation $g(K)$, its three edge labels, in any order, are $(g(K)+1,g(K)+1,g(K))$. The unique edge labeled $g(K)$ is its reference edge.

To bisect $K$, join the midpoint of its reference edge to the opposite vertex. The two resulting triangles have generation $g(K)+1$. In each child, the two new half-edges and the bisector receive label $g(K)+2$; the one inherited nonreference edge retains label $g(K)+1$ and is the child's reference edge. A finite bisection forest is the collection of the initial triangles and all descendants reached by finitely many such bisections; its leaves form a triangulation when all shared-edge subdivisions agree. The admissible family $\mathbb T(\mathcal T_0)$ consists of the matching conforming leaf triangulations generated by these compatible bisections. A refinement $\mathcal T\le\mathcal T_*$ means every cell of $\mathcal T_*$ lies in a cell of $\mathcal T$.

The compatible initial labeling is a hypothesis, not a consequence of an arbitrary initial triangulation. This definition is two-dimensional and makes no claim about three-dimensional closure or complexity.

derivations.claim: Write the parent vertices as $A,B,C$, with reference edge $AB$, midpoint $M$, and squared side lengths $X=|AC|^2$, $Y=|BC|^2$, $Z=|AB|^2$. The two first children have edge-length squares $\{X,Z/4,W\}$ and $\{Y,Z/4,W\}$, where $W=|(A+B)/2-C|^2=(2X+2Y-Z)/4$ by expanding the squared norm. The four labeled types have squared edge lists $\{X,Y,Z\}$, $\{Z/4,X,W\}$, $\{Z/4,Y,W\}$, and $\{X/4,Y/4,W\}$. In type 1 the reference side has square $X$, and the new median square is $(2(Z/4)+2W-X)/4=Y/4$; its children therefore have side lists $\{X/4,Z/4,Y/4\}$ and $\{X/4,W,Y/4\}$, which are a quarter-scale type 0 and type 3. The type 2 calculation interchanges $X,Y$. In type 3 the reference side has square $W$, and its median square is $(2(X/4)+2(Y/4)-W)/4=Z/16$; its children are quarter-scale types 1 and 2. Type 0 gives types 1 and 2 by the first bisection. Hence this finite list is closed under every labeled bisection and no other normalized shape occurs.

Each of the finitely many normalized triangles in step 1.1 is nondegenerate: its area is half the parent area at each bisection and its side lengths are the explicit midpoint lengths, so its three angles are positive. The minimum of these finitely many angles and the initial minimum angle is positive. Hence all descendants have a common positive minimum angle and a common shape-regularity bound. The angle minimum over this finite list is positive; the maximum shape-regularity constant over it and the initial cells is therefore finite.

After the first generation the midpoint $M$ of $AB$ is present. The second generation bisects $AC$ and $BC$, adding their midpoints $N$ and $P$. The four second-generation triangles have reference edges on the segments $AM, BM, CM$; the third generation bisects those segments, in particular $CM$, adding its midpoint $S$ in the interior of $ABC$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $1<p<\infty$ and $p'=p/(p-1)$. For each facet $F$ of
$\widehat S_d$, restriction of smooth functions extends uniquely to a
bounded linear trace map
$$\gamma_F:W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R)\to L^p(F;\mathbb R).$$
For real-valued $u\in W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d)$ and
$G\in W^{1,p'}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R^d)$, the facet traces satisfy
$$\int_{\widehat S_d}u\,\operatorname{div}G+\nabla u\cdot G\,dx =\sum_{F\subset\partial\widehat S_d}\int_F\gamma_Fu\,\gamma_FG\cdot\widehat n_F\,dS.$$
Here $\gamma_FG$ is the componentwise trace and $\widehat n_F$ is the
outward unit normal. The bounded C1-domain trace and Green theorems are not
used for the simplex.

Orient every top-dimensional cell of a matching simplicial mesh by the
ambient orientation of $\mathbb R^d$, and orient each facet by the induced
boundary convention of [[def-oriented-simplicial-cell-chains]]. In the sum
of the oriented boundaries of all top-dimensional cells, every interior
facet occurs twice with opposite signs; every boundary facet occurs once.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

real-valued scalar member of the conforming piecewise-polynomial space in
[[def-broken-and-conforming-polynomial-spaces]]. Then $v\in W^{1,p}(\Omega)$.

affine simplicial mesh, let $1\le p<\infty$, and let $v$ be a real-valued

facet. Then

trace characterization is used.

$\widehat F$ be any facet, and let integer $m\ge0$. For $1\le p,q\le\infty$ there is a finite

respect to the $L^q(\widehat S_d)$ norm.

regularity bound, such that
$$c h_K\le s_{\min}(A_K)\le \|A_K\|\le C h_K, \qquad c h_K^d\le\det A_K\le C h_K^d.$$

A compatible labeled initial mesh is a finite matching affine simplicial triangulation $\mathcal T_0$ of a polygon in $\mathbb R^2$ as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]; matching means distinct cell interiors are disjoint and any shared boundary is a complete common facet. with labels on its edges such that each triangle has one edge labeled $0$ and two labeled $1$, and every shared edge has the same label from both incident triangles. For a descendant triangle of generation $g(K)$, its three edge labels, in any order, are $(g(K)+1,g(K)+1,g(K))$. The unique edge labeled $g(K)$ is its reference edge.

To bisect $K$, join the midpoint of its reference edge to the opposite vertex. The two resulting triangles have generation $g(K)+1$. In each child, the two new half-edges and the bisector receive label $g(K)+2$; the one inherited nonreference edge retains label $g(K)+1$ and is the child's reference edge. A finite bisection forest is the collection of the initial triangles and all descendants reached by finitely many such bisections; its leaves form a triangulation when all shared-edge subdivisions agree. The admissible family $\mathbb T(\mathcal T_0)$ consists of the matching conforming leaf triangulations generated by these compatible bisections. A refinement $\mathcal T\le\mathcal T_*$ means every cell of $\mathcal T_*$ lies in a cell of $\mathcal T$.

Sum the lower bound from step 3.3 over new cells and interchange the two finite sums. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice for the $L^2$ and Sobolev conventions of [[def-countable-choice]].

All functions and data are real-valued. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded polygon and let $\mathcal T$ be a finite conforming matching triangulation by nondegenerate affine triangles, with maximum shape-regularity constant $\Gamma$. Write $h_K=\operatorname{diam}K$ and $h_E=\operatorname{diam}E$. Let $V(\mathcal T)$ be the continuous, piecewise-affine zero-boundary subspace of [[def-broken-and-conforming-polynomial-spaces]], which lies in $H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ by [[thm-matching-continuous-piecewise-polynomials-are-wkp]] and [[thm-zero-boundary-piecewise-polynomials-in-w10p]]. The exact weak model is
$$-\Delta u+b\cdot\nabla u=f,\qquad u\in H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R),\quad f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R),\quad b\in\mathbb R^2\ \text{constant}.$$
The weak form is $\int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla v+(b\cdot\nabla u)v\,dx=\int_\Omega fv\,dx$ for every $v\in H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. The case $b=0$ is the symmetric Laplace model. Given $U\in V(\mathcal T)$, its cell residual is $R_K(U)=f|_K-b\cdot\nabla(U|_K)$; this is $f+\Delta U-b\cdot\nabla U$ because $\Delta U=0$ on each cell. For an interior edge $E=K^+\cap K^-$ define the outward flux jump
$$J_E(U)=\nabla U|_{K^+}\cdot n_{K^+}+\nabla U|_{K^-}\cdot n_{K^-},$$
where $n_{K^\pm}$ are the unit outward normals. Set
$$\eta_K(U)^2=h_K^2\|R_K(U)\|_{L^2(K)}^2+\frac12\sum_{E\subset\partial K,\ E\ {\rm interior}}h_E\|J_E(U)\|_{L^2(E)}^2,$$
and $\eta(U,\mathcal S)^2=\sum_{K\in\mathcal S}\eta_K(U)^2$ for $\mathcal S\subset\mathcal T$. The factor $1/2$ assigns each interior-edge contribution once globally. Let $\Pi_K^0$ be the $L^2(K)$ projection onto constants. The cell data oscillation is
$$\operatorname{osc}_K(U)^2=h_K^2\|R_K(U)-\Pi_K^0R_K(U)\|_{L^2(K)}^2,\qquad \operatorname{osc}(U,\mathcal S)^2=\sum_{K\in\mathcal S}\operatorname{osc}_K(U)^2.$$
Since $b\cdot\nabla U$ is constant on $K$, this oscillation equals $h_K^2\|f-\Pi_K^0f\|_2^2$.

For a separate definitional interface, consider the symmetric diffusion model $-\operatorname{div}(A\nabla u)=f$, where $A$ is a symmetric uniformly elliptic matrix field in the sense of [[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]] and is Lipschitz on each cell. Its cell residual for a piecewise-affine $U$ is $R_K^A(U)=f+\operatorname{div}(A\nabla U)$, and its outward conormal-flux jump is the sum of $A\nabla U\cdot n_K$ from the two incident cells. Let $\Pi_E^0$ be the $L^2(E)$ projection onto constants. The projected edge term $h_E\|J_E^A-\Pi_E^0J_E^A\|_{L^2(E)}^2$ records nonconstant conormal flux. The reliability, contraction, and complexity results authored here concern $A=I$ only; this extension supplies notation and no coefficient-dependent theorem.

Assume Countable Choice, as in the Sobolev trace and inverse-estimate suppliers.

Let $\mathcal T$ be a conforming shape-regular triangular mesh, let $u\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ solve the model of [[def-afem-p1-residual-estimator-and-data-oscillation]], and let $U\in V(\mathcal T)$ be its exact P1 Galerkin solution. There are constants $C_{\rm rel},C_{\rm eff}$ depending only on the shape bound and $|b|h_{\max}$ such that
$$\|\nabla(u-U)\|_2^2\le C_{\rm rel}\eta(U,\mathcal T)^2,$$
and for every $K\in\mathcal T$,
$$\eta_K(U)^2\le C_{\rm eff}\left(\|\nabla(u-U)\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}^2+ \operatorname{osc}(U,\omega_K)^2\right),$$
where $\omega_K$ is the union of $K$ and its edge neighbors. If $\mathcal T_*\ge\mathcal T$ refines every cell in $M\subset\mathcal T$ by three generations and $U_*$ is the exact fine Galerkin solution, then
$$\eta(U,\ M)^2\le C_{\rm eff}\left(\|\nabla(U_*-U)\|_{L^2(\omega(M))}^2+ \operatorname{osc}(U,\omega(M))^2\right),$$
with $\omega(M)$ the union of edge-neighbor patches of marked cells. All constants are independent of the refinement level.

Assume Countable Choice, as in the zero-boundary Sobolev convention.

Let $\mathcal T_H\le\mathcal T_h$ be nested conforming meshes and let $U_H,U_h$ be exact P1 Galerkin solutions for the constant-convection model of [[def-afem-p1-residual-estimator-and-data-oscillation]]. Write $e_j=u-U_j$ and $d=U_h-U_H$. For $b=0$,
$$\|\nabla e_h\|_2^2=\|\nabla e_H\|_2^2-\|\nabla d\|_2^2.$$
For constant $b$, assume the explicit dual-pickup bound
$$\|e_h\|_{L^2}\le C_D h_0^s\|\nabla e_h\|_{L^2}$$
for the nested sequence, with $s>0$, where $h_0=\max_{K\in\mathcal T_0}\operatorname{diam}K$, and put $\mu=C_Dh_0^s|b|<1$. Then
$$\|\nabla e_h\|_2^2\le(1-\mu)^{-1}\|\nabla e_H\|_2^2-\|\nabla d\|_2^2.$$
The dual-pickup bound is an additional hypothesis. It is not asserted for every polygon or mesh.

Assume Countable Choice, as in the Sobolev interpolation suppliers.

Let $\mathcal T\le\mathcal T_*$ be conforming P1 meshes with exact Galerkin solutions $U,U_*$. Let $\mathcal R=\{K\in\mathcal T:K\text{ is subdivided in }\mathcal T_*\}$ and let $\omega(\mathcal R)$ be the union of the vertex stars of cells in $\mathcal R$. Then
$$\|\nabla(U_*-U)\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2\le C\sum_{K\in\mathcal R}\eta_K(U)^2,$$
where $C$ depends on shape regularity, $|b|h_{\max}$, and the local interpolant constants.

For two compatible conforming NVB descendants $\mathcal T_1,\mathcal T_2$ of the same initial mesh $\mathcal T_0$, the union of their bisection forests defines a smallest common conforming overlay $\mathcal T_1\oplus\mathcal T_2$ and
$$\#(\mathcal T_1\oplus\mathcal T_2)\le\#\mathcal T_1+\#\mathcal T_2-\#\mathcal T_0.$$

derivations.claim: Let $\mathcal T^+=\mathcal T\oplus\mathcal T_*$ and let $U,U_*,U^+$ be the exact Galerkin solutions. Best approximation on the overlay gives $e_{\mathcal T^+}\le e_{\mathcal T_*}\le\lambda e_\mathcal T$. By [F2], $\|\nabla(U^+-U)\|_2^2=e_\mathcal T^2-e_{\mathcal T^+}^2\ge(1-\lambda^2)e_\mathcal T^2.$ By [F3], this correction square is at most $C_{\rm loc}\eta_\mathcal T(\mathcal R)^2$, where $\mathcal R$ is the set of coarse cells subdivided in $\mathcal T^+$. By [F1], $\eta_\mathcal T^2\le C_{\rm eff}e_\mathcal T^2$. Combining proves $\eta_\mathcal T(\mathcal R)^2\ge\theta_*\eta_\mathcal T^2$. If $e_\mathcal T=0$, then the comparison condition and all indicators are zero and the empty set is Dörfler.

The bulk algorithm sorts nonnegative weights in decreasing order. Among all sets of a fixed size $m$, the first $m$ sorted weights have maximal sum: replacing any omitted larger weight for a selected smaller one cannot decrease the sum, and repeating yields the prefix. Therefore the shortest prefix reaching threshold $\theta_E\eta_\mathcal T^2$ has minimum cardinality among all Dörfler sets. Since $\mathcal R$ is such a set whenever $\theta_E\le\theta_*$, $|M_E|\le|\mathcal R|$. The overlay cardinality bound [F4] gives $|\mathcal R|\le\#\mathcal T^+-\#\mathcal T\le\#\mathcal T_*-\#\mathcal T_0$.

$$|v|_{W^{\ell,p}(K)} \le C h_K^{m-\ell+d(1/p-1/q)}|v|_{W^{m,q}(K)},$$

abla d\|_2^2$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let
$a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ be linear in its first argument, conjugate-linear
in its second, bounded by $M$, and coercive with constant $\alpha>0$:
$$|a(v,w)|\le M\|v\|_V\|w\|_V,\qquad \operatorname{Re}a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2.$$
Let $F:V\to\mathbb K$ be bounded and conjugate-linear, and let $V_h\subseteq V$
be finite-dimensional. Then there are unique $u\in V$ and $u_h\in V_h$ with
$$a(u,v)=F(v)\quad(v\in V).$$
$$a(u_h,v_h)=F(v_h)\quad(v_h\in V_h).$$
The solutions satisfy
$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le\frac M\alpha\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_V.$$
The real bilinear case uses linear functionals and reads $\operatorname{Re}$ as
the identity.
